title: [review] project-LICHEN-5pe7: PRK derivation chain deviates from RFC 9528
description: In the EDHOC implementation, PRK_3e2m is just an alias for PRK_2e (`self._prk_3e2m = self._prk_2e`) and PRK_4e3m is an alias for PRK_3e2m. Per RFC 9528 sections 4.1.3.2-4.1.3.3, PRK_3e2m should be derived as EDHOC-KDF(PRK_2e, TH_2, "3e2m", ...) and PRK_4e3m as EDHOC-KDF(PRK_3e2m, TH_3, "4e3m", ...). The protocol still works because each KDF call uses distinct labels ("MAC_2", "K_3", etc.) and both initiator and responder implement the same shortcut, so interop is preserved. However, the test vector PRK values (prk_2e == prk_3e2m == prk_4e3m) are not byte-for-byte with a correct RFC 9528 implementation. Files: `python/src/lichen/crypto/edhoc.py` lines 399, 432, 617, 683; `test/vectors/edhoc.json` lines 15-17.

title: [review] project-LICHEN-6mij.2.4: authorize_mutating passes plain_buf to unprotect even when NULL
description:
The doc comment for coap_oscore_authorize_mutating says 'plain_buf: Buffer for decrypted payload (may be NULL if no payload expected, e.g. DELETE)'. However, the implementation always passes plain_buf at line 285 to coap_oscore_unprotect_request, which dereferences it as uint8_t* payload in its function signature (with _Nonnull annotation actually). coap_oscore_unprotect_request passes this to memcpy (unprotect path) and/or writes to it.

If coap_oscore_authorize_mutating were ever called with plain_buf=NULL and an OSCORE-protected request with a payload, coap_oscore_unprotect_request would crash writing to NULL.

Fix: Either:
1. Remove the 'may be NULL' claim from the doc and require non-NULL always (simplest, matches actual behavior)
2. Guard the unprotect call: only call coap_oscore_unprotect_request if plain_buf != NULL and plain_buf_len > 0

Affected file: lichen/subsys/lichen/oscore/coap_oscore.c lines 242-309, and the header doc at coap_oscore.h lines 156-162.

- In edhoc_responder_export_oscore: same pattern at line 1555 and 1564.

Not a correctness bug (harmless overwrite) but confusing dead code. Remove the first assignment on line 1040 and line 1555.

description:
The doxygen comment for lichen_coap_oscore_respond in coap_oscore.h:127 says '@param[in] ctx OSCORE security context (may be NULL)' but the declaration at line 136 annotates ctx as _Nonnull. The implementation doesn't handle NULL ctx — it passes it straight to coap_oscore_protect_response which also expects non-NULL. The doc and annotation are inconsistent.

Fix: update the doc to say '(must be non-NULL)' or remove the '(may be NULL)' qualifier.

title: [review] project-LICHEN-6mij: coap_oscore.c:337 stack buffer CONFIG_COAP_SERVER_MESSAGE_SIZE (stack, not static) in lichen_coap_oscore_respond for every error path
description: lichen_coap_oscore_respond at coap_oscore.c:337 allocates `uint8_t buf[CONFIG_COAP_SERVER_MESSAGE_SIZE]` on the stack. This is used for every OSCORE-protected error response (4.00, 4.29, 5.00, etc.). On constrained devices (STM32WL: 64KB RAM), a 1KB+ stack allocation in every error path is wasteful. All other respond functions use static buffers. Consider making this static to match the project pattern.

title: Gateway: Bridge LICHEN messaging to IRC
description: Implement a gateway-hosted bidirectional bridge between authenticated LICHEN CoAP messaging and IRC. Map explicitly configured LICHEN groups/realms to IRC channels; relay LICHEN /msg/inbox messages through a gateway bot; and convert authorized IRC messages into LICHEN unicast fanout or the future authenticated group-delivery profile. Support conventional IRC networks such as Libera.Chat and Yggdrasil-internal IRC without making IRC authoritative for routing, trust, configuration, SOS, or protocol control.
design: Treat IRC strictly as an application adapter. Preserve verified LICHEN native /128 origin metadata in a stable displayed form without impersonating arbitrary IRC accounts. Require explicit channel/group mappings and inbound account/hostmask authorization. Use persistent message IDs and bridge-instance IDs for loop suppression and reconnect deduplication. Bound queues, message length, attachment behavior, and per-origin/channel rates; apply fair queuing and backoff under IRC flood controls. Validate UTF-8 and sanitize IRC control codes, CTCP, mentions, and command-like content. Keep IRC credentials in protected runtime configuration and never place them in messages or logs. Do not bridge routing/control traffic. SOS and other privileged application operations are disabled unless a later separately reviewed policy explicitly enables them. Prefer IRCv3 message tags for provenance when negotiated, with a readable text prefix fallback. Provide store-and-forward across LoRa or IRC outages without inventing a second messaging identity system.
acceptance_criteria: A gateway connects over TLS to a configurable IRC server and joins configured channels; authenticated LICHEN messages appear once in the mapped channel with origin and timestamp provenance; authorized IRC messages reach the intended LICHEN recipients through the native messaging contract; unauthorized users/channels, malformed content, oversized messages, and protocol-control attempts are rejected; bidirectional loops and duplicates remain suppressed across reconnect and process restart; rate limits, bounded queues, retry/backoff, secret redaction, and outage store-and-forward are tested; simulator integration demonstrates at least two LICHEN nodes and one IRC channel in both directions; a physical-radio demonstration is recorded after the underlying packet/messaging path exists; documentation clearly states that IRC is non-authoritative and describes deployment, mapping, moderation, privacy, and failure behavior.

title: Renode multi-node delivery is non-deterministic (time-model sync across independent Renode processes)
description: After yot8 (async SX1262 RX) + the sim record_reception fix, inter-node LoRa delivery in the Renode mesh WORKS: two t_echo nodes propagate frames and the sim logs deliver_packet abundantly, and sim.metrics.receptions goes >0. BUT it is NON-DETERMINISTIC: across repeated runs of test_mesh_rx (poll up to 60s), some runs see many deliveries (pass in ~15-28s) and others see ZERO over a full minute. Root cause is the bridge/time-model interaction (old r7h4.7): each Renode node is a separate process with its own wall-clock, and lichen-sim advances time / delivers packets across them without a hard sync barrier, so a node's RX window and the other's TX don't always line up. test_mesh_rx is therefore marked xfail(strict=False) - it exercises + documents the path and xpasses when nodes sync, but cannot be a hard CI gate until delivery is made deterministic (e.g., a real time-sync barrier between the Renode nodes and the sim medium, or a lock-step time model). test_mesh_boots + test_mesh_tx (single-node) remain hard-green.

title: Firmware: implement spec §18.2 position resources (/sensors/location, /pos, /pos/cache) in SenML+CBOR
description:
The Rust client now has a spec-faithful SenML Position codec (lichen-client pos.rs, commit ca03c292; spec 12-apps §18.2), and lichen-cli 'position show' targets /sensors/location. But NO firmware node exposes these resources yet — only the gateway's binary /inbound/location POST (inbound_coap.c, a versioned binary format, NOT SenML) exists. To make position sharing actually work end-to-end:
- GET /sensors/location -> application/senml+cbor {bn=urn:dev:mac:<eui>:, bt, lat/lon/alt/speed/heading} (§18.2.2)
- PUT /pos (beacon, §18.2.1) + GET /pos/cache {positions:[{node,lat,lon,alt,ts,age_s}]} (CBOR, not SenML)
Zephyr has no SenML lib; the C side would need a small SenML+CBOR encoder (or reuse zcbor with the RFC 8428 integer labels bn=-2,bt=-3,n=0,u=1,v=2). Until this lands, the client position codec is validated by its own unit tests only (no live node). Consider whether to also expose the existing binary /inbound/location as a client op vs standardizing on SenML.

title: Renode Boot+TX: puck firmware produces 0 LoRa transmissions into lichen-sim (SX1262 model/bridge)
description:
renode.yml 'Renode nRF52840 Boot + TX' now builds and boots (test_mesh_boots PASSES) after the 3iwp board/build fix, but test_mesh_tx FAILS: 'No LoRa transmissions reached lichen-sim' (metrics.transmissions==0 after 10s).

DIAGNOSIS: not a firmware-cadence issue. puck main.c:544 sets last_tx_ms=-BEACON_INTERVAL_MS so the first send_beacon()/lora_send() fires on the first main-loop iteration (~sub-second after boot), well inside the test's 10s window. So the firmware IS attempting to beacon; the TX is not propagating through the Renode SX1262 peripheral model / bridge into lichen-sim's medium. Alternatively the SX1262 driver may not reach 'ready' in Renode and the puck enters an error k_sleep loop (still shows as 'booted'/running, so test_mesh_boots passes).

The test docstring references beads project-LICHEN-r7h4.6 (SX1262.cs RX one-shot at SetRx) and r7h4.7 (bridge/time-model interaction unresolved) as the tracking issues, but neither exists in the current tracker.

NEEDS: local Renode 1.16.1 + the mesh harness (lichen/boards/renode/nrf52840_lichen/test_mesh.py) to reproduce, then trace lora_send -> SX1262.cs -> bridge -> lichen-sim medium. Determine whether TX ever propagates; if the SX1262 Renode model genuinely cannot emit TX into the medium, mark test_mesh_tx xfail with this bead ref (honest, not a test-weakening) rather than forcing green.

Was masked until now: renode.yml boot+TX build always failed first (phantom nrf52840_lichen board + missing west update), so test_mesh_tx never ran in CI before b65e5078.
close_reason: FIXED and verified locally on Renode 1.16.1: pytest test_mesh.py --board=t_echo --nodes=2 -> 2 passed reliably. Root cause was a 4-part chain: (1) firmware never booted (MCUboot slot-0 app, _vector_table at 0x32200 not 0x0) -> seed VTOR/SP/PC via $vt monitor var (58532e3d/684cd1fc); (2) spun forever in nrf_usbd_common_enable (no USB host in Renode) -> disable native USB+mcumgr for Renode builds (e95fc0b9); (3) test waited 10s but puck holds iface down for a 10s USB-settle -> wait 20s (e95fc0b9); (4) SX1262.cs WaitForRxResponse blocked the SPI bus inside Transmit() while in RX, so a node could never leave RX to transmit (both nodes deadlocked) -> made RX async via a background reader thread dispatching TX_DONE/RX_PACKET/RX_TIMEOUT to IRQ flags (08b9c4a5). The SX1262/r7h4 RX-model attribution in the old test comment was a symptom, not the cause; the real blockers were boot+USB+the blocking RX read.

title: Renode CI jobs reference non-existent board 'nrf52840_lichen' — 2 jobs red
description:
Two CI jobs fail because they 'west build -b nrf52840_lichen', but nrf52840_lichen is NOT a real Zephyr board — lichen/boards/renode/nrf52840_lichen/ contains only Renode platform files (support/nrf52840_lichen.repl, .resc), the multi-node harness (test_mesh.py, run_multi_node.py, conftest.py), and a README. No board.yml/board.cmake/dts/Kconfig.board exists, so board resolution fails with 'Invalid BOARD' (boards.cmake:244). Confirmed via git: the commit that added it (3adc8cc2 'feat(renode): add board definitions') only added README + Renode .repl/.resc + Python harness + C# peripherals — never a Zephyr board definition.

Affected jobs:
1. .github/workflows/renode.yml 'Renode nRF52840 Boot + TX' — was failing on SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH='0' (fixed in PR #2 to use the commit ts); now reaches board resolution. Changed -b to t_echo/nrf52840 (PR #2) which resolves the board, but then the puck app's Kconfig for the Renode console overlay/conf mismatches (CONFIG_LICHEN_NATIVE assigned y got n, ZCBOR/MCUMGR warnings-as-errors) — the renode_console.conf/overlay path is stale post-HWMv2.
2. .github/workflows/renode-firmware.yml 'Build Zephyr Firmware' — builds lora_ping and puck for -b nrf52840_lichen (invalid board), plus later steps reference build/lora_ping ELF.

Pre-existing infrastructure breakage from the HWMv2 migration, unrelated to the agent-fleet code or the T1000-E work. Fix requires reworking the Renode CI to build the ELF for a REAL nRF52840 board (e.g. the actual t_echo/nrf52840 or a dedicated nrf52840dk/nrf52840) that the Renode .repl/.resc platform models, then load that ELF in Renode. NOT VALIDATABLE in the current sandbox (no Renode installed). The T-Echo Renode console path also needs its overlay/conf refreshed for the current puck Kconfig.
close_reason: Board/build root cause fixed & confirmed green in b65e5078. renode-firmware.yml 'Build Zephyr Firmware' + single/multi-node jobs: SUCCESS (was building phantom -b nrf52840_lichen; now t_echo/nrf52840 + renode_console overlay/conf + new lora_ping t_echo zephyr,lora overlay + SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH). renode.yml 'Renode Platform Validation': success. renode.yml 'Renode nRF52840 Boot + TX' now builds+boots (test_mesh_boots PASSES) after fixing the west-update-on-cache-hit module drop. The remaining test_mesh_tx failure (0 LoRa transmissions into lichen-sim) is a DISTINCT emulation-layer issue in the SX1262 Renode model/bridge, refiled as yot8 — not a board problem. Neither job references the non-existent board anymore.

title: Multi-peer pinning is unaffordable on nRF52840: constant-time all-peers Schnorr verify keeps radio un-armed
description: peer_try_all_pubkeys verifies EVERY demodulated frame against ALL pinned peers (constant-time, no early exit even after a match). On the 64 MHz nRF52840 each Schnorr-48 verify is slow, and the LoRa RX thread does not re-arm lora_recv() during processing - so every ambient frame makes the radio deaf for N_peers verifies. Measured on the bench 2026-07-17: T-Echo with 1 pinned peer in 3-node RF = 6/14 CoAP round trips; with 2 pinned peers = 0/24 (both directions healthy at L2, responses simply never demodulated). Gateway (ESP32-S3 @ 240 MHz) handles 2 peers fine. Related: 3 ACTIVE nodes at SF10 exceed the ALOHA airtime budget (~45% offered load with the deaf T1000-E retransmitting every cycle + its responses) - see conf comments in lichen/apps/*/boards/. Options: (a) allow early-exit iteration in dev mode (timing side-channel is a non-issue for INSECURE bench provisioning), (b) cheap pre-filter before verify (e.g. try the peer whose window/last-seen matches first - still verify-all on miss), (c) re-arm the radio before verification (queue frames, verify out of RX path - needs RAM), (d) CSMA/backoff + duty limits for airtime. The multi-peer dev provisioning feature itself works and stays; the confs pin single peers on nRF52840 until this is addressed.
close_reason: HARDWARE VALIDATED 2026-07-17. Re-pinned two peers on the T-Echo (gateway ee45..f281 first as the CoAP destination, then the sibling T1000-E 8a1a..2cab), rebuilt + reflashed. With the dev-mode early-exit fix the round trip now sustains 6/9 (67%) over a 2-min window — versus 0/24 (0%) measured with two peers BEFORE the fix. The verify-cost starvation is resolved: matched frames (gateway responses) exit the peer loop after the first Schnorr verify instead of always running all N with the radio un-armed. Ordering gateway-first means its responses exit on iteration 1. The remaining ~33% loss is the separate 3-node SF10 airtime contention (deaf T1000-E free-running + retransmits), a known limitation noted in this bead, not verify cost. link_crypto + ping_l2 unchanged; secure (non-dev) builds keep the constant-time all-peers scan.

title: CBOR map keys not in canonical order per RFC 8428
description:
File: lichen/subsys/lichen/senml/senml.c
Lines: 193-206

CATEGORY: PROTOCOL

RFC 8428 Section 6 states: 'implementations SHOULD sort keys in numeric order by the key value.'

The CBOR label values are:
  SENML_LABEL_BT = -3  (Base Time)
  SENML_LABEL_BN = -2  (Base Name)

Canonical CBOR ordering requires smaller integers first, so -3 should come before -2.

But encode_record() encodes in this order:
  Line 194: SENML_LABEL_BN (-2) first
  Line 202: SENML_LABEL_BT (-3) second

This violates the SHOULD (not MUST) for canonical CBOR ordering.

IMPACT:
- Interoperability: some strict receivers may reject or misparse
- Determinism: non-canonical encoding means identical data may produce different bytes
- Signing: if CBOR payload is signed, non-canonical form complicates verification

FIX: Reorder encoding to emit keys in numeric order:
  SENML_LABEL_BT (-3) before SENML_LABEL_BN (-2)
  Then SENML_LABEL_N (0), SENML_LABEL_U (1), SENML_LABEL_V/VB (2/4), SENML_LABEL_T (6)
notes: Fixed CBOR key ordering in encode_record() to ensure SENML_LABEL_BT before SENML_LABEL_BN per RFC 8428. Count and encoding now both follow numeric key order. Tests pass.
close_reason: CBOR map keys reordered for canonical numeric order per RFC 8428 §6. Updated count logic to match encoding order. Verified with existing test vectors.

title: senml: core::error::Error impl requires nightly or recent stable
description:
File: rust/lichen-senml/src/cbor.rs
Lines: 40-47

The CborError type implements core::error::Error:
```rust
impl core::error::Error for CborError {
    fn source(&self) -> Option<&(dyn core::error::Error + 'static)> {
```

core::error::Error was stabilized in Rust 1.81.0 (September 2024). Before that, no_std crates needed to either:
1. Use the error_in_core feature flag (nightly)
2. Depend on a compatibility crate
3. Only implement std::error::Error behind a feature flag

The Cargo.toml shows no MSRV (minimum supported Rust version). If the project needs to support Rust < 1.81, this implementation would fail to compile.

Impact: Compilation failure on Rust < 1.81.0

Fix: Either:
1. Document MSRV >= 1.81.0 in Cargo.toml: `rust-version = "1.81"`
2. Gate the impl behind a feature flag for older Rust versions
notes: Commit: bc7652090

title: protocol.py: UnicodeDecodeError not wrapped as ProtocolError
description:
File: python/src/lichen/sim/protocol.py
Lines: 146, 156, 688

decode_register and decode_err use .decode('utf-8') which can raise UnicodeDecodeError for invalid UTF-8 sequences:

    sim_id = data[offset : offset + sim_id_len].decode('utf-8')
    node_id = data[offset : offset + node_id_len].decode('utf-8')
    msg = data[2 : 2 + msg_len].decode('utf-8')

Callers (e.g., node_server.py line 269) only catch ProtocolError, not UnicodeDecodeError. A malicious client sending invalid UTF-8 causes an unhandled exception that bubbles up to the generic exception handler rather than returning a proper error response.

Fix: Wrap .decode() calls in try/except UnicodeDecodeError and re-raise as ProtocolError.

Impact: Malformed messages cause unhandled exceptions instead of proper error responses.

title: receive() returns None for all validation failures without distinction
description:
File: python/src/lichen/link/link_layer.py:383-494

The receive() method returns None for many different failure modes:
- Line 411: Radio timeout (expected, not an error)
- Line 420: Malformed frame
- Line 428: Unsigned frame rejected by policy
- Line 436: Payload too short for signature
- Line 454: Unknown sender or bad signature
- Line 469: Key change detected (SECURITY ALERT)
- Line 475: MIC verification failed
- Line 494: Replay detected

Callers cannot distinguish between:
1. Normal timeout (no traffic)
2. Malformed/corrupted frames (hardware issue?)
3. Security violations (attack in progress?)

The logger.warning() calls provide detail, but programmatic callers need to:
- Count security violations for alerting
- Distinguish timeout from rejection for protocol state machines
- Detect key-change attacks

Consider: Return an enum/error type instead of None, or at least distinguish timeout (None) from rejection (specific error).
close_reason: Fix already implemented: receive() now returns ReceiveError enum values to distinguish different failure modes (MALFORMED, UNSIGNED, ENCRYPTED, BAD_SIGNATURE, KEY_CHANGE, REPLAY, NOT_FOR_US, CAPACITY_EXHAUSTED) instead of None for all failures. None is returned only for timeout. Tests exist for all error types.

title: RplOption.to_bytes() doesn't validate type range
description:
File: python/src/lichen/rpl/messages.py:73-80

The RplOption.to_bytes() method doesn't validate that the option type fits in a single byte. If type > 255, the bytes() call will raise an OverflowError at runtime.

Current code:
```python
def to_bytes(self) -> bytes:
    if self.type == RplOptionType.PAD1:
        if self.data:
            raise RplError("Pad1 option carries no data")
        return b"\x00"
    if len(self.data) > 0xFF:
        raise RplError(f"option data too long: {len(self.data)} bytes")
    return bytes([self.type, len(self.data)]) + self.data  # type not validated
```

While RplOptionType enum values are all < 256, the type field accepts any int. An RplOption created with type=256 would fail with an unclear error from bytes().

Fix: Add explicit validation:
```python
if not 0 <= self.type <= 255:
    raise RplError(f"option type out of range: {self.type}")
```
close_reason: Fix already in place at messages.py:86-87. Verified by tests (55 passed) and manual validation.

title: Deprecate node_server.py in favor of RenodeServer
description: NodeServer (node_server.py) uses poll-based RX with 1ms sleep loop. RenodeServer (renode_server.py) has push-based RX. Migrate all usages of NodeServer to RenodeServer, update SimulatorServer.get_node_server_port to spawn RenodeServer instances, then delete node_server.py.

Architecture analysis: NodeServer handles MSG_REGISTER/MSG_RX/MSG_TIME/MSG_CAD for SimRadio clients. RenodeServer uses a simpler per-node protocol (MSG_TX/MSG_RX_ENTER/MSG_RX_EXIT only, fixed node_id). Migration requires either: (1) extending RenodeServer to handle all messages, or (2) changing SimRadio to use per-node connections. This is a design decision, not a drop-in replacement.
Progress: Fixed push-based RX_ENTER handler in NodeServer to use background simulation driver instead of polling.

Changes:
1. Added _sim_driver_task field and _simulation_driver() background task to NodeServer
2. Added _ensure_simulation_driver() to start driver on first node registration
3. Refactored _handle_rx_enter() to await event instead of polling loop
4. Added deprecation notes to poll-based _handle_rx() and _await_rx_result()
5. Updated module docstring to reflect current state

The push-based RX path (used by SimRadio) now uses proper event-driven I/O. The legacy poll-based MSG_RX handler still polls but is deprecated - SimRadio already uses RX_ENTER.

All tests pass (test_node_server.py, test_integration.py, test_sim_client.py, test_server.py, test_multinode.py).

Remaining work:
- Deprecate MSG_RX entirely (remove from protocol, update tests to use RX_ENTER)
- Consider unifying NodeServer with RenodeServer architecture
- This now unblocks project-LICHEN-906e (RX_POLL removal) for the push-based path
Additional progress: Converted test_node_server.py tests to use push-based RX_ENTER.

Changes:
- Updated TestNodeServerRx tests to use encode_rx_enter, MSG_RX_PACKET, MSG_RX_TIMEOUT_PUSH
- Removed poll-based imports (encode_rx, decode_rx_ok, MSG_RX_OK, MSG_RX_TIMEOUT) from test_node_server.py
- All 758 sim tests pass

Remaining poll-based RX usage:
- node_server.py _handle_rx() method (deprecated, for backward compatibility)
- test_protocol.py (tests the protocol encoding API itself, not runtime usage)

This significantly unblocks project-LICHEN-906e. The only remaining runtime poll-based usage is the deprecated _handle_rx handler which could be removed if there are no external clients using MSG_RX.

title: [CR] CoAP client.rs: content_format encoding creates stack arrays that are immediately dropped
close_reason: False positive. The content_format() method at codec.rs:511-521 is correct Rust code. The local array bytes lives on the stack for the entire function scope. The borrow value is passed to self.option() which immediately copies the data to the output buffer via write_option(). Rust's borrow checker guarantees this is safe - if there were a lifetime issue, the code would not compile. The array is not immediately dropped; it persists until after the copy completes. This is a standard Rust idiom for passing temporary slices.

title: Codereview pass 2: TcpServer init - list sharing semantics
description:
Pass 2 reviewed list sharing behavior:

**Finding: Acceptable design**

The connections list is passed to TcpServer by reference, not copied. This means:
- The closure and TcpServer share the same list object
- Modifications in the closure (append/remove) are visible in TcpServer
- Modifications via TcpServer.close() (clear) are visible to the closure

This is intentional and correct for connection tracking. The alternative (copying the list) would break connection management.

The TcpServer dataclass has default_factory=list for connections, but this only applies when serve() does not pass an explicit connections argument. Since serve() always passes the shared list, this works correctly.

No bugs found in this pass.
close_reason: Code review finding already resolved. The bead has closed_at set (2026-07-06T17:19:06) with close_re

title: Codereview pass 2: Identity.__del__ - Consider try/except alternative

title: Codereview pass 1: MockRng SAFETY comment justifies data races rather than ruling them out
description:
Location: rust/lichen-embassy/src/mock.rs:146-151

The SAFETY comment claims data races are 'acceptable' rather than establishing they cannot occur. Rust's UB rules don't have an 'acceptable data race' exception - a data race on static mut is UB regardless of consequence severity.

Better justification would be:
- Assert single-threaded usage is enforced (e.g., #[cfg(not(test))] compile_error on multi-threaded test frameworks)
- Or use AtomicU64 with Relaxed ordering (zero overhead on most platforms)
- Or acknowledge UB risk explicitly: 'SAFETY: We accept potential UB from data races because...'

Current comment reads as if 'acceptable outcome' justifies unsafe, which sets a bad pattern.

Priority: P3 - The risk is real but low (test-only code, single-threaded in practice). The comment exists and mostly explains the reasoning.
close_reason: Issue already fixed: MockRng now uses Mutex<u64> (line 166) instead of static mut. No SAFETY comment justifying data races exists in current code. All mock tests pass.

title: [ipv6_addr.c:88-91] lichen_sha256 error handling hides error code details
description:
Gap: The lichen_sha256 call at line 88 returns a negative errno, but the error message only logs %d which doesn't distinguish failure modes.

What: Line 88-91 check lichen_sha256 return value. The error is logged as 'SHA-256 error %d' but lichen_sha256 only returns 0 or -EIO (per lichen_util.c). The caller cannot distinguish between init/update/final failure.

Why it matters: If SHA-256 fails during pubkey-to-IID derivation, debugging requires knowing which stage failed. The conflated error handling in lichen_sha256() (lines 27-30 in lichen_util.c) returns -EIO for any failure. Adding context to the log message or returning more specific errors would improve debuggability.
close_reason: Won't fix P3: lichen_sha256 returning only -EIO is intentional simplification. SHA-256 failure is extremely rare (hardware fault) and distinguishing init/update/final stages provides minimal debug value. The error code is logged. If SHA-256 fails, the system has bigger problems. Refactoring lichen_sha256 for this edge case adds complexity without proportional benefit.

title: [lora_l2.c:91-109] lora_transition unconditionally forces ABORTED on invalid transition
description:
Gap: Invalid state transitions force ABORTED state even when the caller might handle the error gracefully.

What: Lines 91-109 define lora_transition() which forces ABORTED state on any invalid transition. This is a fail-safe design, but it means programming errors (calling start() twice, etc.) permanently require deinit/init cycle even when the operation could simply fail with an error.

Why it matters: While fail-safe is appropriate for hardware failures, programming errors that cause invalid transitions could be handled more gracefully. For example, calling start() when already running should just return -EALREADY without corrupting state. The current design conflates 'unexpected state' with 'hardware fault'.
close_reason: Intentional fail-safe design: The ABORTED state on invalid transitions is defensive by design (see comment lines 83-84). The state machine treats programming errors as requiring full reinitialization to ensure consistent state. This conflation of 'unexpected state' with 'hardware fault' is intentional - both require operator attention and deinit/init cycle. Graceful handling of double-start() would hide bugs.

title: [cross-file] tx_mutex not protected during lichen_l2_reinit_after_abort()
description:
Interaction: lichen_l2.c:lichen_l2_reinit_after_abort <-> lora_l2.c:lichen_lora_l2_deinit

Bug: lichen_l2_reinit_after_abort() only reinitializes rx_mutex (line 1621). But tx_mutex can also be corrupted if:
1. RX thread is aborted while in lora_rx_callback()
2. Callback calls lichen_l2_input()
3. lichen_l2_input() is pure rx_mutex user (no tx_mutex)

Wait - let me check... Actually lichen_l2_input() only acquires rx_mutex (line 1656). The tx_mutex is only used in lichen_l2_send() and lichen_l2_enable(). The RX thread never acquires tx_mutex.

However, the RX callback path (lora_rx_callback -> lichen_l2_input) acquires rx_mutex. If the RX thread is aborted while holding rx_mutex (inside lichen_l2_input), then rx_mutex is corrupted.

The issue: lichen_l2_reinit_after_abort() is called from lichen_lora_l2_deinit() AFTER line 874. But lora_l2_deinit() at lines 766-768 acquires tx_buf_mutex and at line 834 reinits lora_mutex. It does NOT check if tx_buf_mutex is corrupted.

Actually tx_buf_mutex is different from tx_mutex (lichen_l2.c). They're separate mutexes in separate modules. lora_l2.c has tx_buf_mutex for TX buffer protection. lichen_l2.c has tx_mutex for tx_ipv6_buf/tx_frame_buf protection.

So the issue is: if the RX thread was aborted while in lichen_l2_input, rx_mutex is corrupted. lichen_l2_reinit_after_abort() correctly reinits rx_mutex. But the RX thread doesn't hold tx_mutex, so no issue there.

Actually this is NOT a bug. The code is correct. Withdrawing this finding.
close_reason: False positive: tx_mutex (lichen_l2.c) is separate from tx_buf_mutex (lora_l2.c). RX thread only acquires rx_mutex in lichen_l2_input(), never tx_mutex. tx_mutex is only used by TX path (lichen_l2_send) and enable/disable. RX thread abort cannot corrupt tx_mutex.

title: [lichen_l2.c:548-549] lichen_link_rx called multiple times for same frame
description:
What: peer_try_all_pubkeys() iterates through all peers and calls lichen_link_rx() for each one to try signature verification. This means lichen_link_rx() is called N times for each incoming frame, where N is the number of active peers.

Why it matters: This is the intended design (documented in comment at line 475), but has performance implications:
1. Each call to lichen_link_rx() performs SCHC decompression
2. Each call performs MIC verification (AES-CCM or CRC32)
3. Only signature verification differs between iterations

The performance impact is bounded by CONFIG_LICHEN_LINK_MAX_NEIGHBORS (max 64). At LoRa speeds, this overhead is acceptable, but it's not optimal.

Alternative design: Parse frame once, extract signature, try pubkeys against signature only. This would reduce redundant work.

Marking as code smell/optimization opportunity rather than bug.
close_reason: Added inline BY DESIGN comment at line 548 explaining that repeated lichen_link_rx calls are intentional for peer signature verification. The comment references the issue ID and explains the performance tradeoff (redundant SCHC/MIC work acceptable given LoRa's low packet rate and bounded peer count).

title: [lichen_l2.c:1806] rx_mutex held during potentially-blocking allocation
description:
What: lichen_l2_input() holds rx_mutex from line 1656 until line 1832, including during net_pkt_rx_alloc_with_buffer() which can block for CONFIG_LICHEN_L2_RX_ALLOC_TIMEOUT_MS (default 50ms).

Why it matters: If the system is under memory pressure:
1. RX callback enters, acquires rx_mutex
2. net_pkt allocation blocks for up to 50ms
3. Any other operation needing rx_mutex (peer_add, peer_remove, enable/disable) blocks

At LoRa data rates, this is unlikely to cause starvation, but the design holds the mutex longer than necessary.

Evidence: k_mutex_lock at 1656, net_pkt_rx_alloc at 1806-1808, k_mutex_unlock at 1832.
close_reason: Documented as known trade-off in lichen_l2.c. Comment explains: holding mutex during allocation prevents races, timeout bounds blocking to 50ms max, LoRa data rates make contention acceptable.

title: [lora_l2.c:723] lichen_lora_l2_deinit has TOCTOU race in state check
description:
Contract: lichen_lora_l2_deinit should atomically transition from STOPPED/ABORTED to DEINITING.
Violation: Lines 725-753 read state, then check various conditions with if/else-if chain, creating a window between state read and lora_transition_from() calls. A concurrent thread could change state in this window (though unlikely in embedded context).
Impact: Low in practice - embedded systems typically single-threaded for this type of operation. The CAS in lora_transition_from() catches most races. However, the pattern is not consistent with the atomic discipline used elsewhere.
Mitigation: The existing lora_transition_from() CAS provides sufficient protection. Document that concurrent deinit() calls are not supported.
close_reason: False positive: while the code reads state then checks it (TOCTOU pattern), lora_transition_from() uses atomic_cas() internally which atomically verifies the expected state. If state changes between lora_get_state() and the CAS, the CAS fails safely. The initial read is just an optimization to select which expected-state to try. Added SECURITY comment documenting why this is safe.

title: [lora_l2.c:366] 1-second backoff on RX error does not account for thread abort timing
description:
Final pass: This was missed because reviewers focused on the consecutive_errors counter and warning threshold, not the sleep interaction with abort.

Root cause: When lora_recv() returns a non-timeout error, the thread sleeps for 1 second:
  k_sleep(K_MSEC(1000));

The stop() function at line 602-616 uses RX_THREAD_QUICK_JOIN_MS (100ms) + RX_TIMEOUT_MS as join timeout. If the thread is in this 1-second backoff sleep when stop() is called:
1. Thread is sleeping for 1000ms
2. stop() waits 100ms + RX_TIMEOUT_MS (default 1000ms)
3. Total potential wait: up to 1100ms after state change
4. But backoff can last full 1000ms, which is within timeout - close margin

If RX_TIMEOUT_MS is configured lower (e.g., 100ms for fast response), the join timeout becomes 200ms and the 1000ms backoff will cause forced abort.

Impact: On persistent LoRa errors, stop() may force-abort the thread unnecessarily because the backoff sleep exceeds the join timeout. This triggers the ABORTED state and requires full deinit/init cycle.

Fix: Either:
1. Make backoff interruptible (use k_sleep with cancellation or poll state in backoff loop)
2. Add backoff duration to join timeout calculation
3. Document the RX_TIMEOUT_MS must be >= 1000ms when error backoff is possible
close_reason: Fixed: Added comprehensive documentation in lora_l2.c rx_thread explaining the 1000ms backoff timing interaction with stop() join timeout, including analysis of why forced abort during error backoff is acceptable behavior for a malfunctioning radio.

title: [lichen_l2.c:507-528] peer_try_all_pubkeys constant-time claim is weak
description:
Round 2 gap analysis: Missed because the constant-time comment looked plausible.

At lines 498-528:
```c
/*
 * SECURITY: Constant-time peer iteration to prevent timing side-channel.
 *
 * Always iterate through ALL peers even after finding a match. This
 * prevents an attacker from inferring which peer index matched based
 * on how quickly the function returns.
 */
int found_idx = -1;
int found_ret = -LICHEN_EAUTH;

for (size_t i = 0; i < CONFIG_LICHEN_LINK_MAX_NEIGHBORS; i++) {
    if (!peer_table[i].active) {
        continue;  // <-- NOT constant-time: skip inactive peers
    }
    ...
```

The comment claims constant-time iteration, but:
1. Inactive peers are skipped (line 508-510), making iteration time depend on active peer count
2. lichen_link_rx() itself is NOT constant-time (signature verification has data-dependent timing)
3. Non-auth errors abort early (line 536)

The 'constant-time' claim is only partially true - it's constant relative to WHICH peer matches (index position), but NOT constant relative to total active peers or signature verification cost.

This isn't necessarily a vulnerability (L2 timing attacks over LoRa are impractical), but the SECURITY comment overstates the protection. A more accurate description would be 'peer-index-independent iteration'.
close_reason: Fixed: Updated comment to accurately describe protection as peer-index-independent iteration with documented limitations

title: [lichen_util.c:27-29] TinyCrypt SHA-256 returns only on NULL which is pre-checked
description: At lines 27-29, the code checks tc_sha256_init/update/final return values, with a comment saying 'TinyCrypt's SHA-256 functions only fail on NULL (checked above)'. But the NULL check is at line 21. If tc_sha256_* functions can ONLY fail on NULL, and we check NULL first, then the checks at lines 27-29 are dead code. The comment acknowledges this. Either trust the library (remove the checks) or don't trust it (keep them). Current code is defensive but the comment reveals it's paranoid defensive. This is fine for crypto code - paranoia is good.
close_reason: Fixed: Updated comment to clarify defensive error handling for defense-in-depth

title: [lichen_l2.c:1549] rx_link_key copied but original may be modified concurrently
description: At line 1549, rx_link_key is copied from link_ctx.link_key while holding rx_mutex. However, the comment says this is to protect against 'future refactor' that moves cleanup outside rx_mutex. The current code holds rx_mutex for the entire lichen_l2_input(), so this is safe. But note that the peer_try_all_pubkeys call at line 1589 releases rx_mutex? No - actually rx_mutex is held continuously. The function is correct but the defensive copy suggests concern about a race that cannot currently occur. The issue is more that link_ctx.link_key could be modified by lichen_l2_enable(disable=true) but that path also acquires rx_mutex, so no race.
close_reason: Fixed: Added issue reference to existing comment explaining the defensive copy is intentional for future-proofing

title: [lora_l2.c:602-616] thread join timeout may be insufficient if lora_recv just started
description: The RX thread join at lines 602-616 uses RX_THREAD_QUICK_JOIN_MS (100ms) then RX_TIMEOUT_MS. The comment at line 608 says 'worst-case lora_recv() just started when we set the stop flag'. But if RX_TIMEOUT_MS is the max, and lora_recv just started, it needs the full timeout. The code adds RX_THREAD_QUICK_JOIN_MS + RX_TIMEOUT_MS which is correct for worst case. However, the log message at line 614 says the thread timed out after the sum, but k_thread_abort is only called if BOTH timeouts fail. This is correct but the message could be clearer. No actual bug here, just noting the timing is tight.
close_reason: Fixed: clarified comment and log message for join timeout behavior

title: [main.c:128] ambiguous return value on goto cleanup path
description: At line 128, when goto cleanup is reached (eui64 == NULL), the return is '(ret < 0) ? ret : -ENODATA'. But ret is never set to negative before the goto at line 108. ret is only set by init/start calls (lines 91, 99), not by get_eui64. So this will always return -ENODATA, making the ternary redundant. Fix: simplify to 'return -ENODATA;' or set ret = -ENODATA before goto.
close_reason: Fixed: set ret = -ENODATA before goto cleanup, eliminating redundant ternary

title: [lichen_l2.c:1586] src_eui64 initialization may hide authentication bugs
description: src_eui64 is defensively initialized to all zeros at line 1586. However, on success of peer_try_all_pubkeys, src_eui64 should be filled by lichen_link_rx(). If there's a bug where src_eui64 is NOT filled on success, the defensive initialization means we'll log/use a zero address without detecting the bug. Consider removing the initialization and adding an explicit check that src_eui64 is not all-zeros after successful authentication, or at least a debug assertion.
close_reason: Fixed: Removed zero-initialization of src_eui64 to make bugs visible if peer_try_all_pubkeys returns success without setting it

title: [lichen_l2.c:430-432] peer table full returns -ENOSPC but no mechanism to evict stale peers
description:
Category not checked: Resource exhaustion handling

Bug found: When the peer_table is full (CONFIG_LICHEN_LINK_MAX_NEIGHBORS reached), lichen_peer_add() returns -ENOSPC with a LOG_WRN but provides no way to recover:

1. No LRU eviction of stale peers
2. No API to query how many peers are active
3. No API to iterate peers for application-level eviction
4. No aging mechanism to remove inactive peers

In a mesh network, peers may join and leave. With default CONFIG_LICHEN_LINK_MAX_NEIGHBORS=16, the table fills quickly and cannot accept new legitimate peers.

The replay_table comment (lines 213-223) discusses a poisoning attack where 'an attacker floods spoofed source addresses to evict legitimate peers' - but currently there's NO eviction at all, which is worse: first 16 peers fill the table permanently.

Impact: P3 - Mesh network eventually becomes unable to accept new peers after 16 are registered.
close_reason: Fixed: Added LRU eviction for peer table. When table is full, the least-recently-seen peer is evicted to make room for the new peer. Added last_seen timestamp field to peer entries, updated on successful frame verification and peer add/update.

title: [lichen_l2] peer_table active flag not zeroed on startup
description:
State machine bug: The peer_table[] static array's active flags are never explicitly initialized to false. They rely on BSS zero-initialization.

While C guarantees static variables are zero-initialized, the peer_table contains pointers to pubkeys and eui64s. If the BSS initialization is ever skipped (e.g., warm restart on some bootloaders), stale peer entries with active=true could persist.

Furthermore, after lichen_l2_enable(false), the peer_table is cleared (lines 791-795). But after lichen_l2_enable(true), there's no re-zeroing if link_ctx was already initialized.

Location: lichen_l2.c:244 (static declaration), lines 791-795 (cleanup in disable)

Recommendation: Add explicit zeroing of peer_table in lichen_l2_iface_init() before any operations, or in lichen_link_init() call path.

Priority: P3 - defense-in-depth, BSS init is reliable on most platforms.
close_reason: Fixed: Added explicit memset() in lichen_l2_iface_init() to zero peer_table at boot. While C guarantees static BSS zeroing, explicit initialization is defensive and documents the invariant.

title: [lichen_l2] iface_init fail path mutex ordering differs from enable path
description:
Cross-file potential deadlock: The fail_late_init cleanup path in lichen_l2_iface_init() only acquires rx_mutex (line 1030), while lichen_l2_enable() acquires tx_mutex THEN rx_mutex (lines 695-696 for enable, 778-779 for disable).

Current safety: During iface_init, the interface is not yet operational - no concurrent TX should be possible since lichen_iface is only set at line 975, and the RX callback is only registered at line 978. So there's no practical race.

Future hazard: If code is refactored to allow early TX (e.g., during boot for neighbor discovery), the inconsistent lock ordering could cause ABBA deadlock between:
- fail_late_init path: rx_mutex only
- concurrent TX: tx_mutex only (or tx_mutex then rx_mutex if refactored)

Location: lichen_l2.c:1028-1034 (fail_late_init) vs lines 695-696, 778-779 (enable)

Recommendation: For consistency, fail_late_init should acquire tx_mutex then rx_mutex, matching lichen_l2_enable(). Even if currently safe, consistent lock ordering prevents future bugs.
close_reason: Fixed: fail_late_init path now acquires both tx_mutex and rx_mutex in the correct order (tx_mutex first, then rx_mutex), matching the enable/disable paths in lichen_l2_enable(). Updated comment to document the lock ordering rationale.

title: [lichen_l2.c:1204-1207] net_pkt_rx_alloc timeout configurable but default may be too long
description: Function: lichen_l2_input. Resource allocation: The net_pkt allocation uses CONFIG_LICHEN_L2_RX_ALLOC_TIMEOUT_MS (line 1207). If this timeout is long (e.g., seconds), the RX thread blocks while holding rx_mutex, preventing other operations. The mutex is released only after allocation completes or times out. If the packet pool is exhausted and timeout is long, this could cause significant delays. The Kconfig should document the tradeoff. Priority 3 - configuration guidance, not a bug in default values.
close_reason: Verified: timeout already configurable via CONFIG_LICHEN_L2_RX_ALLOC_TIMEOUT_MS (default 50ms, range 0-1000ms) with documented tradeoffs in Kconfig help. Code at line 1367-1369 properly references this config with explanatory comment.

title: [lora_l2.c:184] rx_thread does not check aborted state in loop
description: Function: rx_thread (static). Thread safety: The RX thread loop condition (line 218) only checks 'atomic_get(&lora_state.running)'. If the module enters aborted state (lora_state.aborted = 1) but running is not cleared, the thread continues. In practice, stop() sets running=0 before or after setting aborted=1, so this is a non-issue. But checking aborted in the loop condition would make the thread exit faster when abort is signaled. Priority 3 - theoretical race, not a practical bug.
close_reason: Fixed: Added documentation comment explaining that checking LORA_RUNNING is sufficient because LORA_ABORTED can only be set after the RX thread is already terminated. The shutdown sequence in stop() is: (1) transition to STOPPED, (2) join/abort thread, (3) only then transition to ABORTED. So the thread exits gracefully on STOPPED or is forcibly terminated before ABORTED is ever set.

title: [lichen_l2.c:640] lichen_l2_enable acquires both mutexes with nested locking
description: Function: lichen_l2_enable. Thread safety: The function acquires tx_mutex then rx_mutex (lines 695-696 enable path, 778-779 disable path). The comment at lines 687-692 documents this ordering. However, if any future code acquires rx_mutex then tx_mutex (ABBA pattern), deadlock would occur. The code currently maintains consistent ordering but no static analysis enforces this. Consider adding a comment at mutex definitions or using Zephyr's lock ordering annotations if available. Priority 3 - correctly ordered, documentation improvement.
close_reason: Fixed: added lock order documentation at mutex definitions (~line 217) with canonical LOCK ORDER comment explaining tx_mutex must be acquired before rx_mutex. Updated comments in lichen_l2_enable() to reference the canonical location. Lock order was already consistent across all call sites - this fix documents it properly.

title: [ipv6_addr.c:193] lichen_ipv6_addr_to_str truncation check after snprintf
description: Function: lichen_ipv6_addr_to_str. Contract violation: The function checks buflen < LICHEN_IPV6_ADDR_STR_LEN at line 200 but then checks for truncation again at line 235. The first check should prevent the second from ever triggering, but the second check exists 'defensively'. The issue is that if snprintf returns a value >= buflen (truncation), the buffer contains truncated output which the function then reports as an error. A caller might have already logged the partial output. Consider zeroing buf on truncation error (currently only zeroed on ret < 0). Priority 3 - defensive code, minor inconsistency.
close_reason: Duplicate of .10 - same snprintf truncation pattern

title: [lora_l2.c:713] lichen_lora_l2_get_eui64 returns alias with no thread safety
description: Function: lichen_lora_l2_get_eui64. Contract violation: Returns a pointer to internal state (lora_state.eui64) without mutex protection. The header documents this (line 176: 'The returned pointer aliases internal state. Do NOT modify. Contents are stable after init() completes.'). However, if deinit() is called while a caller holds the pointer, the eui64 buffer could be reused. Since eui64 is not zeroed in deinit() and init() only writes it once (idempotent), this is safe in practice. Priority 3 - design note for future maintainers.
close_reason: Fixed: Added thread safety documentation to lichen_lora_l2_get_eui64() in both header (lora_l2.h) and implementation (lora_l2.c). The function returns an alias to internal state; callers must ensure no concurrent deinit() while using the pointer, or copy the value immediately.

title: [lichen_l2.c:911] lichen_l2_iface_init no error return
description: Function: lichen_l2_iface_init. Contract violation: The function has void return type but can fail in multiple ways (LoRa init, EUI-64 retrieval, link addr set). It sets iface_init_failed flag internally but callers (NET_DEVICE_INIT) cannot detect failure. Zephyr's net_if_api.init is defined as void, so this is by design, but downstream operations (send, enable) must check iface_init_failed to avoid operating on half-initialized state. The implementation correctly does this (lines 539, 649), so this is documented behavior, not a bug. Priority 3 - design observation only.
close_reason: Documented: Zephyr's net_if_api.init callback mandates void return. Error handling via iface_init_failed atomic flag is correct; added @note documenting this design constraint.

title: [lichen_util.h:74] secure_zero memcpy volatile cast may not prevent optimization
description: In secure_zero() line 74, __builtin_memcpy is used to write zero words, followed by a volatile read-back on line 76 to prevent optimization. However, the read-back only reads one byte '*(volatile uint8_t *)p' rather than the entire word that was written. A sufficiently smart compiler might realize that only the first byte needs to be preserved and optimize away stores to the other bytes. Consider reading back the full word or using volatile for all writes. The current approach is likely safe in practice but not formally guaranteed.
close_reason: Duplicate of .9 - same secure_zero function

title: [ipv6_addr.c:235] snprintf truncation check uses ret as size_t comparison
description: In lichen_ipv6_addr_to_str() line 235, '(size_t)ret >= buflen' checks for truncation. This is correct but the cast is needed because ret is int. However, we already know ret >= 0 from line 226 check, so the cast is safe. The real issue is that snprintf returns the number of characters that WOULD have been written, not the actual count. If buflen is 39 and ret is 39, we wrote 39 chars but no null terminator (truncation). The >= check is correct but a clarifying comment would help future readers understand why >= not >.
close_reason: Verified correct: The code at line 235 is the standard snprintf truncation check pattern. After line 226 checks ret<0 (error case), line 235 safely casts ret to size_t for comparison with buflen. The cast is safe because we've already ensured ret>=0. Build passes without warnings.

title: lichen_l2_recv function exists comment could be clearer
description:
In lichen_l2.c:259-269, the comment explains why lichen_l2_recv exists:

```c
/*
 * WHY THIS EXISTS (even though it just returns NET_CONTINUE):
 * Zephyr's net_if_recv_data() unconditionally calls iface->l2->recv() without
 * a NULL check. If we omit this callback from NET_L2_INIT, any packet injection
 * via net_recv_data() would dereference NULL and crash. This function must exist
 * even when it performs no L2-specific processing. Compare Zephyr's dummy L2
 * (subsys/net/l2/dummy/dummy.c) which follows the same pattern.
 */
```

This is good defensive documentation. However, the function name `lichen_l2_recv` could mislead readers into thinking it does receiving, when actually it is the callback invoked AFTER a packet has been received and before it goes to the IP layer.

What goes wrong: Someone searching for "where does RX happen" might look at this function and be confused when the actual RX path is in `lichen_l2_input`.

Suggested fix: Consider renaming to `lichen_l2_rx_filter` or `lichen_l2_pkt_intercept`, or add a one-liner clarifying the call context: "Called by net_recv_data() after lichen_l2_input() injects a packet."
close_reason: No change needed. The existing docstring and inline comment are already clear: explains WHY the function exists (Zephyr requires non-NULL l2->recv callback), references the source (net_if_recv_data), compares to Zephyr's dummy L2 pattern, and explains the return value rationale. Comment quality is good as-is.

title: Packet ownership semantics clearly documented
description:
The codebase consistently documents packet ownership semantics:

**lichen_l2.h header comment (lines 15-20):**
```c
/*
 * Packet ownership (Zephyr net_l2 contract):
 * - TX (L2 send): On success (return 0), L2 takes ownership of net_pkt and
 *   calls net_pkt_unref(). On error (return < 0), caller retains ownership.
 * - RX (lichen_l2_input): Allocates a new net_pkt and passes ownership to
 *   the network stack via net_recv_data().
 */
```

**lichen_l2_send (lines 298-301):**
```c
/*
 * Ownership: Per Zephyr net_l2 contract, on success (return 0) this function
 * takes ownership of @p pkt and calls net_pkt_unref(). On error (return < 0),
 * caller retains ownership and is responsible for cleanup.
 */
```

**lichen_l2_input (lines 848-856):**
```c
/*
 * Inject into the network stack.
 *
 * Ownership semantics:
 * - On success (ret >= 0): net_recv_data takes ownership of pkt.
 *   The network stack will unref the packet when processing completes.
 *   We MUST NOT access or unref pkt after this point.
 * - On failure (ret < 0): We retain ownership and must unref pkt.
 */
```

This documentation prevents use-after-free and double-free bugs that are notoriously hard to debug in networking code.
close_reason: Positive finding - no action needed, documents good practice

title: Idempotent init functions with clear documentation
close_reason: Positive finding - no action needed, documents good practice

title: Log level policy is documented and consistently applied
description:
lichen_l2.c:47-58 documents the log level policy:

```c
/*
 * Log level policy:
 *   LOG_ERR: Initialization failures, resource exhaustion, programming errors
 *            (NULL params), conditions that prevent operation.
 *   LOG_WRN: Transient conditions that drop a single packet but do not indicate
 *            system failure - e.g., RX during early startup, frame auth failure,
 *            oversized frame. These are expected in normal mesh operation...
 *   LOG_INF: State transitions, initialization success, configuration summary.
 *   LOG_DBG: Per-packet tracing, detailed state.
 */
```

This policy is then followed consistently:
- NULL parameter errors use LOG_ERR
- Packet drops (frame too short, auth failure) use LOG_WRN
- Init success and enable/disable use LOG_INF
- Per-packet tracing uses LOG_DBG

Having an explicit policy prevents log spam from normal mesh conditions (which include authentication failures from misconfigured peers) while ensuring serious errors are visible.
close_reason: Positive finding - no action needed, documents good practice

title: ipv6_addr.h struct in6_addr detection cascade lacks summary
description:
In ipv6_addr.h:31-79, there is a long preprocessor cascade for detecting struct in6_addr. The rationale comments are excellent (lines 36-54), but the actual #if/#elif chain spans 23 lines with no summary of what each branch does.

What goes wrong: When adding support for a new platform, a developer must trace through each condition to understand where their platform falls. The block would benefit from a summary table.

Suggested fix: Add a brief structured comment before the cascade:
```c
/*
 * Detection order:
 *   1. LICHEN_HAVE_IN6_ADDR       - explicit user override
 *   2. IN6ADDR_ANY_INIT           - POSIX-compliant header included
 *   3. CONFIG_NET_IPV6 + Zephyr   - include zephyr/net/net_ip.h
 *   4. Platform header guards     - system in6_addr already defined
 *   5. Fallback                   - provide our own
 */
```
close_reason: Added structured table documenting all 5 detection priority levels with their checks, actions, and use cases

title: LICHEN_LORA_FRAME_OVERHEAD derivation comment is confusing
description:
In lora_l2.h:69-71, the constant is defined as:

```c
#define LICHEN_LORA_FRAME_OVERHEAD   55  /* 57 raw - 2 margin = 5 hdr + 4 MIC + 48 sig - 2 */
```

The comment arithmetic is confusing:
- "57 raw - 2 margin" suggests 57 is the baseline
- "5 hdr + 4 MIC + 48 sig" = 57, which checks out
- But then "-2" is applied, yielding 55

However, the derivation in the docstring above (lines 46-67) explains the 2-byte margin differently: it is reserve space for SCHC rule ID and future address fields.

What goes wrong: The inline comment arithmetic is trying to show two things at once. A reader has to reconcile "57 raw - 2" with "5+4+48 - 2".

Suggested fix: Simplify the inline comment to just reference the derivation above:
```c
#define LICHEN_LORA_FRAME_OVERHEAD   55  /* See derivation in docstring above */
```
close_reason: The confusing comment has already been fixed. The constant at line 79 is now defined symbolically as (5 + SCHNORR48_SIG_LEN + 2) with a clear inline comment, and a detailed 30-line derivation block (lines 45-77) explains each component. Both production copies (lichen/subsys/lichen/l2/lora_l2.h and firmware/bridge-zephyr/subsys/lichen/lora_l2.h) have been updated.

title: LICHEN_LORA_FRAME_OVERHEAD derivation not fully shown
description:
lora_l2.h lines 44-56 define LICHEN_LORA_FRAME_OVERHEAD as 55 with a comment:

```c
/**
 * @brief MTU for LICHEN LoRa interface
 *
 * Derivation (must match lichen/schnorr48.h and frame format):
 *   Max LoRa payload at SF10/BW125:     255 bytes
 *   LICHEN frame overhead:               ~10 bytes (length, flags, epoch, seqnum, addr, mic)
 *   Schnorr-48 signature:                 48 bytes (SCHNORR48_SIG_LEN)
 *   Margin for SCHC rule ID:               ~2 bytes
 *   ----------------------------------------
 *   Available for IPv6 payload:          ~195 bytes, rounded to 200
 */
#define LICHEN_LORA_MAX_PHY_PAYLOAD 255
#define LICHEN_LORA_FRAME_OVERHEAD   55  /* 10 + 48 - margin rounded */
#define LICHEN_LORA_MTU (LICHEN_LORA_MAX_PHY_PAYLOAD - LICHEN_LORA_FRAME_OVERHEAD)
```

The inline comment '10 + 48 - margin rounded' = 58 - margin, which doesn't equal 55. The derivation shows ~10 + 48 + ~2 = ~60, not 55.

lichen_l2.c lines 132-153 attempt to validate this with BUILD_ASSERTs but use LICHEN_FRAME_BASE_OVERHEAD (9 bytes, not 10) plus signature (48), totaling 57, still not 55.

What goes wrong: The claimed derivation doesn't match the constant. A maintainer cannot verify correctness.

Improvement: Either fix the derivation arithmetic to show how 55 is actually computed, or adjust the constant to match the derivation.
close_reason: The LICHEN_LORA_FRAME_OVERHEAD derivation is now fully documented in lora_l2.h lines 45-79. The comment provides a complete byte-by-byte breakdown: 5 bytes header (length + LLSec flags + epoch + sequence) + SCHNORR48_SIG_LEN (48 bytes) + 2 bytes headroom = 55. The macro uses symbolic constants: (5 + SCHNORR48_SIG_LEN + 2).

title: NET_L2_MULTICAST_SKIP_JOIN_SOLICIT_NODE requires LoRa broadcast knowledge
description:
lichen_l2.c lines 459-476 return NET_L2_MULTICAST | NET_L2_MULTICAST_SKIP_JOIN_SOLICIT_NODE:

```c
/*
 * NET_L2_MULTICAST: Tells Zephyr this L2 can deliver IP multicast frames.
 * LoRa is inherently broadcast - all transmissions reach all receivers,
 * so multicast delivery works by default.
 *
 * NET_L2_MULTICAST_SKIP_JOIN_SOLICIT_NODE: Skip joining solicited-node
 * multicast groups (ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX). In a broadcast medium, all nodes
 * receive all Neighbor Solicitation messages regardless of multicast group
 * membership, making solicited-node optimization pointless. Skipping the
 * join avoids MLD report traffic that would waste precious LoRa airtime.
 * OpenThread uses the same pattern for similar reasons.
 */
```

This comment is well-written but assumes the reader knows:
1. What solicited-node multicast groups are
2. What MLD is
3. Why LoRa airtime is 'precious'

What goes wrong: A reader without IPv6 NDP knowledge cannot evaluate if the flag is correct.

Improvement: Add a one-line summary before the detail: 'LoRa is broadcast, so multicast filtering happens in software not hardware; we skip multicast group join protocol traffic since all nodes receive all frames anyway.'
close_reason: Implementation exists at lichen_l2.c:1330-1362. The lichen_l2_flags() function returns NET_L2_MULTICAST | NET_L2_MULTICAST_SKIP_JOIN_SOLICIT_NODE with thorough documentation explaining the rationale (LoRa broadcast medium makes solicited-node multicast optimization unnecessary) and design assumptions. Function is registered via NET_L2_INIT at line 1365.

title: main.c LED error pattern undocumented for field debugging
description:
main.c:129-137 blinks LED 3 times on USB failure:
```c
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    gpio_pin_set_dt(&led, 1);
    k_sleep(K_MSEC(100));
    ...
}
```

What goes wrong: A field technician seeing the blink pattern has no way to know what it means without source code access. If additional error patterns are added later, distinguishing them becomes guesswork.

Suggested: Add a comment block at the top of main.c documenting LED patterns:
```c
/*
 * LED diagnostic patterns:
 * - 3 rapid blinks (100ms each): USB CDC initialization failed
 * - Solid on during init: normal startup
 * - Off after init: ready
 */
```

This creates a single reference point for all patterns.
close_reason: Closed

title: lora_l2_stop join timeout logic could use named constants
close_reason: Closed

title: lora_l2.c: k_thread_join timeout sequence comment doesn't explain the 100+5000ms strategy
description:
Location: lora_l2.c:329-341

The stop() function joins with a 100ms timeout, then RX_TIMEOUT_MS (5000ms), then aborts. The comment says 'short initial timeout for the common case where the thread exits quickly'.

What goes wrong: Why 100ms specifically? Is it based on lora_recv() internal timing, expected worst-case for the running-flag check, or arbitrary? Without this context, a future maintainer might change it to 50ms (faster shutdown!) or 500ms (more margin!) without understanding the tradeoff.

Suggested fix: Add one sentence: '100ms is ample time for a thread that checked running between lora_recv() calls; if still blocked, it's inside lora_recv() and needs up to RX_TIMEOUT_MS to return.'
close_reason: Comment already explains the timeout strategy. Header (lora_l2.h:149-153) documents two-phase join: a quick 100ms wait for the common case, then up to RX_TIMEOUT_MS if the thread is blocked in lora_recv(). Implementation (lora_l2.c:385-401) provides detailed rationale for both phases and worst-case justification. Line numbers shifted (bead: 329-341, current: 385-401) indicates prior edits addressed this.

title: Good: lichen_l2.c ownership comments on TX/RX packet handling
description:
Locations: lichen_l2.c:148-152, 628-634

The comments documenting Zephyr net_pkt ownership semantics are valuable:
- TX (line 148-152): 'On success (return 0), L2 takes ownership... On error (return < 0), caller retains ownership'
- RX (line 628-634): 'On success (ret >= 0): net_recv_data takes ownership... We MUST NOT access or unref pkt after this point'

Why this is good: Packet ownership in Zephyr's net stack is a common source of double-free and use-after-free bugs. These comments make the contract explicit and prevent 'helpful' refactors that add pkt access after handoff. Worth defending if someone suggests removing 'obvious' comments.
close_reason: Pattern documented - no action needed

title: lichen_l2.c: LICHEN_MIN_FRAME_LEN defined inside function body
description:
Location: lichen_l2.c:518

The macro LICHEN_MIN_FRAME_LEN is defined inside lichen_l2_input() using #define, which is unusual placement for a constant.

What goes wrong: Reader expects #defines at file scope. When scanning the file for constants, this one is invisible. Harder to audit the frame format logic when the relevant constant is buried mid-function.

Suggested fix: Move to file scope near MAX_LORA_FRAME (line 40) with a comment explaining derivation: length(1) + flags(1) + src_eui64(8) + mic(4) = 14.
close_reason: LICHEN_MIN_FRAME_LEN is now defined at file level in lichen_l2_internal.h:64 under a Constants section

title: Good: atomic_t guards with explicit memory semantics comments
description: lichen_l2.c:71-75 and :444-445 document the acquire/release semantics of atomic_set/get for link_ctx_initialized. This explains why the atomics are sufficient without a full mutex - important for future maintainers who might question the pattern.
close_reason: Positive review observation recorded; no implementation action required.

title: Good: Thread-safe callback snapshot pattern
description: lora_l2.c:199-202 snapshots rx_callback and user_data under mutex before invoking. This ensures the callback/userdata pair is consistent even if another thread calls set_rx_callback() concurrently. Clean pattern for decoupling callback registration from invocation.
close_reason: Positive review observation recorded; no implementation action required.

title: Review: zephyr-firmware 2026-06-27
notes:
Review confidence: 15% chance of missed bug.
Least confident areas: 
- LoRa driver interaction (external APIs not in scope)
- Full enable/disable cycle testing (behavioral, not static)
- Edge cases in net_pkt handling with Zephyr internals
Would raise confidence if: integration tests covering disable/enable cycle, fuzzing protocol boundaries.
close_reason: All children complete

title: lichen_l2.c:527-529 comment explains defensive copy but is verbose
description: The comment block at lichen_l2.c:521-529 explaining why rx_link_key is copied rather than pointer-captured is accurate but verbose (9 lines). The code pattern (copy + local pointer) is idiomatic for key material handling. Trim to: '/* SECURITY: Copy key to stack to survive hypothetical cleanup reordering. */'
close_reason: Trimmed verbose ownership comment from 7 lines to 2: 'net_recv_data takes ownership on success; we unref on failure'

title: secure_zero() implementation is correct for its purpose
description: The volatile-pointer secure_zero() pattern (lora_l2.c:44-50, ipv6_addr.c:32-37, lichen_l2.c:32-38) is the standard approach for preventing dead-store elimination. While it could be consolidated into a shared header, the duplication is acceptable for static-inline functions in embedded code where call-site inlining is important.
close_reason: P3 observations acknowledged, no fix needed

title: Thread-safety model in lichen_l2_enable() is well-reasoned
description: lichen_l2.c:247-314: The shutdown sequence (clear callback -> signal thread -> release mutex -> join -> reacquire mutexes -> cleanup) correctly handles the race between in-flight callbacks and cleanup. The comment at lines 279-288 explaining the ordering is accurate. Worth defending if someone proposes 'simplifying' by removing the double-mutex acquisition or moving cleanup earlier.
close_reason: P3 observations acknowledged, no fix needed

title: lichen_l2_input holds rx_mutex across net_pkt_alloc which may block
description:
lichen_l2.c lines 445-538: rx_mutex is held from line 445 until line 538, spanning net_pkt_rx_alloc_with_buffer() (line 520) and net_pkt_write() (line 530). Both may block waiting for memory. This could delay other RX processing if multiple packets arrive rapidly.

However: LoRa at SF10 has ~100ms minimum packet time, so packet bursts are unlikely. The mutex protects rx_ipv6_buf which is shared. Would need double-buffering to improve, which adds complexity.

Verdict: Acceptable for current LoRa data rates. Flag for reconsideration if moving to faster radios.
close_reason: Already fixed. In current lichen_l2_input(), rx_mutex is released at line 1958 BEFORE net_pkt_rx_alloc_with_buffer() (line 1976) and net_pkt_write() (line 1991). The code explicitly copies rx_ipv6_buf to a local buffer before releasing the mutex, then performs blocking packet operations outside the critical section. Comments at lines 1952-1958 and 1968-1971 document this design. The original line numbers (445-538) now contain peer table management functions unrelated to net_pkt allocation.

title: GOOD: Header ipv6_addr.h provides fallback struct in6_addr when CONFIG_NET_IPV6 unavailable
description: ipv6_addr.h lines 35-47: When Zephyr networking is not enabled, defines its own compatible struct in6_addr. This allows the address utilities to be used in standalone mode (testing, non-networked builds). The conditional is clear and the comment explains the purpose.
close_reason: Not a bug - positive observation

title: lora_l2.h tx function takes non-const data pointer despite not needing mutation
description:
lora_l2.h line 114: int lichen_lora_l2_tx(uint8_t *data, size_t len) - the data pointer is non-const. The comment says 'may be mutated by driver' but the actual implementation (lora_send) in Zephyr should not require mutation. If mutation is truly possible, the comment is correct; if not, the signature should be const uint8_t *data for caller clarity.

Verify: Check Zephyr's lora_send() signature. If it takes const, change this to const.
close_reason: Duplicate of project-LICHEN-rwio.22 and project-LICHEN-rwio.34

title: HAVE_LICHEN_LINK macro duplicates CONFIG_LICHEN_LINK check
description:
lichen_l2.c lines 28-35: Defines HAVE_LICHEN_LINK as 1 or 0 based on CONFIG_LICHEN_LINK, then uses #if HAVE_LICHEN_LINK throughout. The indirection adds no value - could use #if defined(CONFIG_LICHEN_LINK) directly.

However, the current pattern does enable writing 'if (HAVE_LICHEN_LINK)' in regular C code (not just preprocessor), which can be useful for avoiding #ifdef in function bodies. Mild style preference, not a bug.
close_reason: Taste: HAVE_LICHEN_LINK macro improves readability over raw CONFIG_ checks; minimal cost, no harm

title: ipv6_addr_to_str does not use zero compression
description:
ipv6_addr.c:145-155 formats IPv6 addresses without RFC 5952 zero compression. A link-local like fe80::1234:5678:abcd:ef01 is printed as fe80:0000:0000:0000:1234:5678:abcd:ef01 (39 chars).

What goes wrong as-is: Log messages are harder to read, copy-paste into other tools may confuse users expecting standard format. For LICHEN's link-local addresses (fe80:: prefix with 4 zero hextets), this is noticeable.

Note: Implementing RFC 5952 compression is more code and not urgent. If a fix is desired, Zephyr provides net_addr_ntop() when CONFIG_NET_IPV6 is enabled, which already implements compression.
close_reason: Not a bug - intentional design decision. Code at ipv6_addr.c:291-296 explicitly documents why uncompressed format was chosen over RFC 5952: (1) deterministic output, (2) simpler parsing for consumers, (3) consistent log line lengths. Header also documents this as intended behavior.

title: Wireshark Lua dissector for LICHEN link frames
description: Write a Wireshark Lua dissector plugin (lichen.lua) that decodes LICHEN link-layer frames captured over UDP/serial. Fields: Length, LLSec byte (Encrypted/Sig/MIClen/AddrMode), Epoch, SeqNum, DstAddr (variable width per AddrMode), SCHC payload, MIC. Should work with DLT_USER captures from the simulator.

title: Web status dashboard (FastAPI + HTMX)
description: Lightweight web dashboard that proxies the node's CoAP resources into a browser UI. FastAPI server makes CoAP requests to a local node and renders status/neighbors/presence/messages. Single-file Python app with embedded HTML template using HTMX for auto-refresh.
